transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess… I came because I can’t get away from this feeling that I’ve failed, especially as a father. And not just that, but like I’m not much use to anyone anymore.

It keeps going around in my head, over and over. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly I’m thinking about all the ways I should’ve done better, and then I remember some little thing from years ago—like a school event I missed, or something I said wrong—and it just turns into this whole proof that I don’t deserve much of a future. I know that sounds dramatic, but it feels very real when it starts.
Have you been feeling this way most days, and has it been going on for at least two weeks straight?

Yeah… most days, I’d say. It’s been about a month now, I think—since my daughter left for college out of state. I keep telling myself that’s supposed to be a good thing, you know, she got in and she’s doing what she should be doing, but the house just felt different after she left, and then my head sort of… went with it. So yes, definitely more than two weeks.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things anymore that used to make you happy, like hobbies or spending time with family?

Yeah… I have. I used to really look forward to working on my model railway—there’s this little station piece I was building, and I had all these plans for the wiring and scenery. I’d lose hours to it before. Now it’s just sitting there half-finished on the table, and I keep walking past it like it belongs to someone else.

And the Cubs games too… my daughter and I used to watch them together, even when they were terrible, which is most of the time, honestly. We had little jokes about it. Now even turning a game on just feels… pointless. Like I can’t quite get myself to care.
Has this lack of enjoyment or interest in things you used to love been happening every day, or does it come and go?

It’s… pretty much every day, I think. I keep hoping it’ll come back if I just sit down with the railway, but the trains are still there half-built on the table and I just sort of stare at them.

And with the Cubs games, I’ll think, well, maybe I’ll put one on like we used to, me and my daughter, but even opening it on TV feels pointless. Then I end up thinking about how she’d know who was batting and I’d make some dumb joke, and—sorry, that’s not really what you asked. But yes, the not caring part is there most days.
Do you find that these feelings are worse in the morning when you first wake up, or do they tend to stay about the same throughout the day?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear pattern like that. Mornings are… I mean, they’re strange because the house is quiet, and I’ll sometimes lie there thinking about what I’m supposed to do with the day, but then later on it’s not like it suddenly lifts or anything I can really point to.

It’s hard to compare, honestly. I haven’t been tracking it. Some days I think, well, maybe mornings are heavier, but then by afternoon I’m still just sort of… in it. So I’m not sure I can say it’s worse at one time.
Have you been feeling more tired or lacking energy lately, even if you haven’t been doing much physically?

Yeah… yes, definitely. It’s not even like I’m out doing yard work or anything. Just carrying a basket of laundry upstairs, I’ll stop halfway and feel ridiculous, like my legs are full of sand or something.

Even sorting the mail—just standing there deciding what’s junk and what isn’t—feels like too much. I’ll put it in a pile and tell myself I’ll come back to it, and then it just sits there. My wife used to tease me because I’d organize the envelopes by size sometimes, which is… I don’t know why I’m telling you that.

But yes. I feel tired even when I’ve been in bed for ages. It’s like moving through wet cement most of the time.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently—like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

Yeah… less, I guess. I don’t really make proper meals most days anymore. I’ll look in the fridge and just… close it again, like it’s some kind of decision I don’t have in me.

Sometimes I forget until it’s late, and then I’ll just have toast or a bowl of cereal. Which is funny, I used to be picky about cereal—my daughter liked the sugary stuff and I’d act like I was above it, then eat half the box anyway. Sorry.

But yes, I’ve lost some weight, I think. I had to tighten my belt another notch recently, so… I suppose that answers it.
Have you been blaming yourself for things more than usual, or feeling like you're a failure or that you don't deserve to be happy?

Yeah… that’s probably the main thing, honestly. I keep coming back to this idea that I failed. As a father, especially. And not just that, but as… I don’t know, as a useful person.

It loops in my head. I’ll be doing something stupid like rinsing a cup, and suddenly I’m thinking about all the ways I should’ve done better. My daughter had this school project once with a cardboard volcano, and I remember getting annoyed because the glue wasn’t drying fast enough—why do I remember that? It’s ridiculous. But those little things stack up, and then it feels like proof of something bigger.

So yes. I feel like I don’t really deserve much of a future sometimes. Not in a dramatic way, I just… I can’t shake the feeling that I’ve used up whatever chance I had to be decent.
Have you had episodes like this before, where you felt down and lost interest in things, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I mean, everyone has bad stretches, don’t they? I’ve had times before where I was low, sure, but whether it was like this… I’m not sure.

I remember once years ago I stopped going to this little book club thing at the library—not because of the books, actually the chairs were awful, these metal folding ones that made your back hurt after twenty minutes—and I told myself I was just busy. Maybe that was something, maybe it wasn’t.

This feels… bigger, I think. Or maybe I’m just noticing it more now. I don’t know. I’m sorry, I’m not giving you a very useful answer.
Can you think back and recall if there was a time before this current period when you felt down nearly every day and lost interest in things you usually enjoy, lasting for at least two weeks or more?

I’m trying to think… I don’t know. Two weeks sounds so specific when you say it like that. I can remember being down before, but whether it was nearly every day and with losing interest in everything… I’m not sure.

Time gets blurry looking back, you know? Like I remember certain odd details—what mug I was using, or the weather, or some stupid argument about where we kept the batteries—but not the shape of the whole thing.

So… I can’t honestly say yes. I also can’t swear it never happened. I just don’t have a clear enough memory of it.
Can you recall if there was ever a time before this current period when you felt down most days and lost interest in things you usually enjoy for more than a couple of weeks?

I’m sorry, I’m still not sure I can pin that down. I know I’ve had low patches before, and I’ve dropped things I used to do, but whether it was most days for more than a couple of weeks… I don’t know.

I keep thinking of these random bits instead of the actual answer—like a period where I stopped listening to this radio program I liked, but then I also remember the host changed and I didn’t like his voice, so maybe that wasn’t me being low, maybe it was just that. It’s hard to separate.

So I can’t honestly say, “yes, that happened before.” I just don’t remember clearly enough.
Can you recall if there was ever a time, lasting several weeks or more, when you felt down most days and stopped caring about things you usually enjoy, even before this current period?

I hear what you’re asking, and I’m trying not to just dodge it. I just… I don’t have a clear memory of a period like that before this one.

There were times I was off, I suppose, where I didn’t feel like myself, and I’d stop doing certain things. But then I start second-guessing why—like maybe I stopped going somewhere because parking was a nightmare, or because someone there annoyed me, or because I was tired. I can remember the stupid details better than the actual mood.

So I can’t really say yes, there was definitely a several-week stretch before where I felt down most days and stopped caring about things. I don’t know. I wish I could give you a cleaner answer.
Can you remember if there was ever a time before your daughter went to college when you felt down most days and stopped caring about things you usually enjoy, lasting several weeks or more?

Before she went to college… I mean, that’s a big marker, so you’d think it would make it easier to remember, but it kind of doesn’t. I remember all the college stuff—boxes in the hallway, buying towels, this ridiculous argument about whether she needed a printer. I can see that more clearly than how I was feeling day to day.

I know there were times I was sad, or quiet, or I didn’t keep up with things the way I used to. But whether it was most days, for several weeks, and whether I really stopped caring about things I normally enjoyed… I can’t say that clearly.

So I don’t want to tell you yes if I’m just filling in gaps. I’m not sure.
Have you ever experienced a period of feeling down most days and losing interest in things you usually care about that lasted for several weeks or more before your daughter went to college?

Before she went to college… I still get muddled on the timing. I can tell you what it’s like now more clearly than what came before that.

Like, I used to really look forward to the model railway stuff, and Cubs games with my daughter—those were actual things I cared about. The trains are still just sitting there half-built on the table, and even turning on a game now feels… I don’t know, pointless. Which sounds silly, because it’s just baseball, but it used to be our thing.

But before she went to college, whether there was a stretch like that for several weeks or more—I honestly can’t pin it down. I don’t want to say yes if I’m just mixing it up with now.

These symptoms broadly suggest depression (F32.9, F33.9), adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.22), or a personality trait or disorder contributing to chronic patterns of thinking (e.g., F60.7). No specific psychotic, manic, anxiety, or trauma-related symptoms were endorsed yet, which reduces immediate suspicion for other categories but further questioning is needed.

The patient has described persistent feelings of failure, guilt, and worthlessness, particularly around missing out on moments with their daughter. These feelings have been present most days for about a month, which rules out adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.22) as the primary issue is more prolonged and consistent with a depressive episode. However, we cannot yet differentiate between a major depressive episode (F32.9) and recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9).

The patient's symptoms have persisted for about a month, and there is evidence of anhedonia (loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities) and persistent negative self-evaluation. This supports the continuation of F32.9 (depressive episode, unspecified) and F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder, unspecified) as candidates. F43.22 (adjustment disorder with depressed mood) is less likely now due to the duration and depth of symptoms, which appear more consistent with a primary depressive disorder.

The patient continues to endorse symptoms consistent with a depressive episode, including persistent low mood, rumination, anhedonia, and duration exceeding two weeks. The differential remains between a single episode of major depressive disorder (F32.9) and recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9), as there is not yet enough information to distinguish between the two.

The patient continues to endorse symptoms consistent with major depressive disorder, including persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, weight loss, and self-blame. The duration of symptoms (at least one month) supports both F32.9 (single episode) and F33.9 (recurrent episodes), but recurrence cannot be confirmed without further history of prior episodes. No new disorders are added or ruled out at this time.

The patient has not provided clear evidence of prior depressive episodes, which is necessary to support the diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9). Therefore, the more specific diagnosis of F32.9 (Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified) is retained based on the current presentation.
